title: “Peekaboo” Dwarf Galaxy HIPASS J1131–31
caption: The Peekaboo dwarf galaxy HIPASS J1131–31, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: HIPASS J1131–31 · constellation Hydra · about About 22 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, Igor Karachentsev (SAO RAS); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A large bright star sits in the middle with four long rays spreading in an X, and between the rays on the right lies a small blue, peanut-shaped galaxy with a few bright spots. That little galaxy is HIPASS J1131–31, nicknamed Peekaboo, about 22 million light-years away in Hydra. The glaring star, TYC 7215-199-1, belongs to our own galaxy.

The foreground star moves quickly across the sky. A century ago it would have sat directly in front of the galaxy, which could not have been detected then. Peekaboo has emerged from behind it only in the past 50 to 100 years.

Hubble resolved about 60 stars in the galaxy, and nearly every one seems to be no more than a few billion years old. That is very unusual nearby, where galaxies typically hold ancient stars. Peekaboo is also extremely poor in elements heavier than hydrogen and helium, so it gives astronomers a close look at conditions usually found only in the distant, early universe.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS took this image. NASA shows F606W in cyan and F814W in orange.
understand.eye: The four long rays around the bright star are an effect of the telescope's optics, not part of the star itself, and the colours are hues assigned to two filters.

explore: The galaxy is only 1,200 light-years across. It was first detected more than 20 years ago as a patch of cold hydrogen by the Parkes radio telescope Murriyang in Australia. The Southern African Large Telescope measured its metal content, and the team plans further study with Hubble and Webb.
